recipe.history:
Brussels sprouts — Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera — take their name from the city of Brussels, Belgium, where they were cultivated extensively in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, though the vegetable likely originated in the broader Mediterranean basin in antiquity. They are miniature cabbages, forming as tight axillary buds along a central stalk, and they belong to the same species as cabbage, kale, broccoli, cauliflower, and kohlrabi — a remarkable species that human agricultural selection has shaped into more distinct forms than almost any other food plant on earth. Brussels sprouts contain glucosinolates, sulfur-containing compounds that, when broken down by heat or chewing, produce the bitter, sulfurous notes that made generations of children recoil from them at the dinner table. But this reputation, in the culinary world of the twenty-first century, has been thoroughly rehabilitated. Roasted at high heat, Brussels sprouts caramelize along their outer leaves, developing a nuttiness and sweetness that transforms the vegetable from a schoolyard villain into a genuinely spectacular ingredient. Shaved thin and dressed as a slaw, they are crisp, slightly spicy, and fresh in a way that no other brassica quite matches.

The rehabilitation of Brussels sprouts as a beloved American vegetable happened gradually across the 1990s and 2000s, accelerated by the farm-to-table movement and by chefs who discovered that high-heat roasting — something home cooks had not traditionally applied to the vegetable — was the key to unlocking its sweeter, nuttier side. By the 2010s, Brussels sprouts had completed their remarkable image transformation from obligatory childhood punishment to the must-order dish at every gastropub and farm-to-table restaurant in the country. The Brussel-Mania Burger channels both preparations of the vegetable — crispy roasted sprouts for texture and caramelized depth, and a shaved slaw for freshness and crunch — creating a burger that makes the case for Brussels sprouts as a genuinely compelling burger topping, not a novelty, but a real improvement.

I hated Brussels sprouts until I was twenty-six years old. This is embarrassing to admit, but it is true, and the shift happened because of a meal at a tiny restaurant in Portland, Oregon, where the chef served them roasted in a very hot oven with bacon fat and a squeeze of lemon, and the outer leaves were black at the edges and the insides were sweet and almost creamy, and I ate an entire bowl of them and felt that I had been lied to my entire childhood — not by the vegetable, but by everyone who had ever boiled it. From that meal forward, I roasted Brussels sprouts constantly, and eventually I started shaving them raw for slaws, and eventually they ended up on a burger, and it was so obviously right that I couldn't believe it had taken me so long to get there. This burger is my apology to Brussels sprouts for the first twenty-six years.

The Brussel-Mania Burger is a burger about transformation — raw to roasted, bitter to sweet, rough to tender — and this theme of transformation runs most powerfully through the patty itself. At medium rare, 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, the beef undergoes exactly the right degree of transformation: the exterior is seared and deeply browned by the Maillard reaction, while the interior remains yielding, rosy, and full of all the moisture and flavor that higher temperatures would drive away. The crispy Brussels sprouts, which have been subjected to intense oven heat to bring out their sweetness, are a perfect textural counterpoint to the tender patty below them. To cook the beef as aggressively as the sprouts are cooked — to apply the same high heat all the way through — would be to misunderstand the whole composition. The beef must be medium rare. The sprouts can be as crispy as you like.
ingredients: 1 large egg beaten with 1 tbsp water, for egg wash
For the crispy roasted Brussels sprouts:
450g Brussels sprouts, halved through the stem
For the shaved Brussels sprout slaw:
300g Brussels sprouts, very thinly shaved on a mandoline or with a sharp knife
fine sea salt and white pepper
softened unsalted butter, for toasting buns
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Combine flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in the stand mixer bowl with dough hook. Add warm milk, water, and egg. Mix, then add butter gradually on medium speed. Knead on medium-high until smooth and elastic, 8 minutes. Rise until doubled, 1 to 1.5 hours. Divide into 6 portions, shape, proof 40 minutes. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Egg wash, sesame seeds, bake 18 to 20 minutes. Cool.

2. Roast the Brussels sprouts: Increase oven to 425°F (220°C). Toss halved Brussels sprouts with olive oil, salt, pepper, and red pepper flakes. Spread cut-side down in a single layer on a rimmed baking sheet — do not crowd them. Roast until the cut sides are deeply caramelized and the outer leaves are crispy and nearly charred, 22 to 25 minutes. Set aside.

3. Make the shaved Brussels sprout slaw: Whisk together apple cider vinegar, olive oil, honey, Dijon, salt, and pepper in a large bowl. Add shaved Brussels sprouts and toss well. Let sit for at least 15 minutes to allow the sprouts to soften slightly and absorb the dressing. Taste and adjust seasoning.
4. Cook the bacon: In a skillet over medium heat, cook bacon until crisp. Drain on paper towels. Keep warm.
5. Make the lemon aioli: Whisk mayonnaise, lemon juice, lemon zest, and grated garlic together. Season with salt and white pepper. Refrigerate until needed.

6. Form the patties: Divide beef into 6 portions (about 150g each). Shape into 4-inch patties, 3/4 inch thick, with a center dimple. Season generously with kosher salt and black pepper just before cooking.

7. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties undisturbed for 3 minutes on the first side. Flip and lay Gruyère slices on each patty. Cook 2 to 2.5 more minutes. Add a splash of water and cover to steam-melt the Gruyère for 30 seconds. The internal temperature must reach 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) — medium rare, the only correct doneness. Rest patties on a rack for 3 minutes.
8. Toast the buns: Butter the cut sides and toast in the skillet butter-side down over medium heat until golden, about 1 minute.

9. Assemble: Spread lemon aioli on both bun halves. Place a generous pile of shaved Brussels sprout slaw on the bottom bun. Place the Gruyère-covered patty on top of the slaw. Lay a strip of crispy bacon across the patty. Top with a heap of crispy roasted Brussels sprouts. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately.
